questions.lo: The English Reformation: Henry VIII and the break with Rome
questions.q: Why did Henry VIII first come into conflict with the Pope in the 1530s?
options: The Pope wanted to invade England
The Pope refused to let Henry end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon
Henry wanted England to join Spain
The Pope closed all of England's schools
questions.explain: Henry wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled so he could marry Anne Boleyn and try for a male heir. When the Pope refused, Henry broke with Rome and made himself head of the Church of England.

questions.lo: The English Reformation: Henry VIII and the break with Rome
questions.q: Which 1534 law made the English monarch, rather than the Pope, the head of the Church of England?
options: The Bill of Rights
The Act of Union
The Act of Supremacy
Magna Carta
questions.explain: The Act of Supremacy (1534) declared the monarch Supreme Head of the Church of England, cutting ties with the Pope in Rome.

questions.lo: Thomas Cromwell and the dissolution of the monasteries
questions.q: Who was Henry VIII's chief minister who organised the break with Rome and the dissolution of the monasteries?
options: Oliver Cromwell
Thomas Cromwell
William of Orange
Thomas More
questions.explain: Thomas Cromwell was Henry VIII's minister in the 1530s. He is often confused with Oliver Cromwell, who led Parliament's army 100 years later during the Civil War.

questions.lo: Thomas Cromwell and the dissolution of the monasteries
questions.q: Give the best reason why the dissolution of the monasteries from 1536 was about more than just religion.
options: It gave the Crown huge amounts of land and wealth
It made England join the Spanish Empire
It gave every peasant the right to vote
It created the first Parliament
questions.explain: As well as removing Catholic institutions, closing the monasteries handed their rich lands and money to the Crown, making Henry far wealthier and letting him reward loyal nobles.

questions.lo: The Elizabethan religious settlement and conflict with Catholics
questions.q: Why is Elizabeth I's Religious Settlement often described as a 'middle way'?
options: It abolished religion completely
It made England Catholic again
It created a Protestant Church but kept some familiar features to try to satisfy most people
It handed power to the Pope
questions.explain: Elizabeth set up a Protestant Church of England but kept some traditional elements, hoping most people could accept it and calm the religious conflict that had torn the country apart.

questions.q: What was the outcome of the Spanish Armada in 1588?
options: Spain successfully conquered England
The Armada was defeated and scattered
The two fleets never met
England surrendered to Spain
questions.explain: The Catholic Spanish fleet was defeated by English tactics (including fireships) and wrecked by storms as it fled around Britain. The victory boosted Protestant England's confidence.

questions.lo: The first colony in America and first contact with India
questions.q: What major change in England's overseas activity began during this period?
options: England stopped all trade with other countries
England founded its first colony in America and made first contact with India
England was invaded and colonised by India
England gave up the sea entirely
questions.explain: This period saw England's first colony in America and first contact with India, marking the beginnings of overseas trade and empire that would grow much larger later.

questions.lo: The causes and events of the civil wars, 1642-51
questions.q: The English Civil War, which broke out in 1642, was mainly a conflict between which two sides?
options: England and Scotland
Catholics and the Pope
King Charles I and Parliament
Rich landowners and poor peasants
questions.explain: The Civil War was a struggle between King Charles I and Parliament over power and religion. It was NOT simply 'rich vs poor' - both Royalists and Parliamentarians had rich and poor supporters.

questions.lo: The causes and events of the civil wars, 1642-51
questions.q: Which belief of Charles I most angered Parliament in the years before the Civil War?
options: That the king should share power equally with everyone
That his power came directly from God (the Divine Right of Kings)
That England should become a republic
That Parliament should control the army
questions.explain: Charles believed in the 'Divine Right of Kings' - that his authority came from God and could not be challenged. This clash over who really held power was a key cause of the war.

questions.lo: The Interregnum: the republic and Oliver Cromwell
questions.q: What happened to King Charles I in 1649?
options: He was crowned king of Scotland
He was put on trial and executed
He fled to France and was never seen again
He signed the Act of Union
questions.explain: In 1649 Charles I was tried and executed - the first time a British king had been legally put to death by his own people. Britain then became a republic called the Commonwealth.

questions.lo: The Interregnum: the republic and Oliver Cromwell
questions.q: What title did Oliver Cromwell take when he ruled Britain during the Interregnum?
options: King of England
Pope of Britain
Lord Protector
Prime Minister
questions.explain: Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector. He held enormous power but was never crowned king, and Britain remained a republic (the Commonwealth) during this kingless period called the Interregnum.

options: The rebuilding of London after a fire
The return of the monarchy, when Charles II became king
The dissolution of the monasteries
The union of England and Scotland
questions.explain: After Oliver Cromwell died and the republic collapsed, Charles I's son was invited back as Charles II in 1660. This return of the monarchy is called the Restoration.

questions.lo: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the power of Parliament
questions.q: In the Glorious Revolution of 1688, who did Parliament invite to take the throne from the Catholic King James II?
options: Oliver Cromwell
The Pope
The Protestant William of Orange and Mary
The King of Spain
questions.explain: Fearing a Catholic, absolute monarchy under James II, Parliament invited the Protestant William of Orange and Mary to rule. James fled, making it a near-bloodless change of monarch.

questions.lo: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the power of Parliament
questions.q: What was the most important long-term result of the Glorious Revolution and the Bill of Rights (1689)?
options: England became a full democracy where everyone could vote
Power shifted from the Crown towards Parliament
The monarchy was abolished forever
The Pope became head of the Church again
questions.explain: The Bill of Rights meant the monarch could no longer rule without Parliament, creating a constitutional monarchy. A common mistake is to think it made everyone able to vote - most people still could not.

questions.q: What did the Act of Union of 1707 create?
options: The Church of England
The Kingdom of Great Britain, joining the English and Scottish parliaments
The first colony in America
The English republic
questions.explain: The Act of Union joined the parliaments of England and Scotland into one, creating the Kingdom of Great Britain governed from Westminster. The two had shared a monarch since 1603 but stayed separate countries until then.

questions.lo: Society, economy and culture across the period
questions.q: Which of these was a feature of society and culture in Britain across this period?
options: Everyone worked in factories
A golden age of theatre (such as Shakespeare), alongside witch trials and growing overseas trade
The internet and printing had ended religious belief
Britain had no contact with any other country
questions.explain: The period saw flourishing theatre, art and literature, but also strong religion and superstition (including witch trials), a mostly rural and poor population, and growing overseas trade with America and India.

questions.lo: Using evidence and explaining cause and consequence
questions.q: A historian uses a diary written by a Puritan during the Civil War. What should they keep in mind?
options: Diaries are always completely accurate
The writer had a viewpoint, so the source may be one-sided
Only official government documents count as evidence
Sources from ordinary people should be ignored
questions.explain: Every source reflects the viewpoint of whoever made it. A Puritan diary is useful but one-sided, so historians always ask who wrote a source, when and why before trusting it.

questions.lo: Using evidence and explaining cause and consequence
questions.q: Which statement best describes how power in Britain changed overall between 1509 and 1745?
options: Power moved from Parliament to the Pope
Power gradually shifted from a strong Crown towards Parliament
Nothing about who held power changed
Kings became more powerful than ever before
questions.explain: The big story of the period is a gradual shift of power from a very strong monarchy (Henry VIII) towards Parliament, especially after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the Bill of Rights.
